definition: A function is continuous at $x = a$ if $f(a)$ exists and $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = f(a)$: near $a$ its graph has no break or jump.
A function is differentiable at $x = a$ if its derivative $f'(a)$ exists there: the graph is smooth at that point, with one tangent and no corner.
A sequence or series is convergent if its terms (or its partial sums) settle on one finite value as $n \to \infty$.
A sequence or series is divergent if it does not converge: its values grow without limit or never settle on one value.
Finding a derivative straight from its definition, $f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h}$, without the differentiation rules.
A derivative found by differentiating more than once; the $n$th derivative is written $f^{(n)}(x)$ or $\frac{\mathrm{d}^{n}y}{\mathrm{d}x^{n}}$.
